title: The Milky Way’s biggest star cluster may be the core of a galaxy it swallowed

cover.alt: A dense field of thousands of red, blue and white stars in the core of the globular cluster Omega Centauri.
cover.credit: NASA, ESA, J. Anderson and R. van der Marel (STScI) · CC BY 4.0

body: Omega Centauri packs about **10 million stars** into a ball roughly 150 light-years across, making it the largest and most massive known globular cluster in our galaxy. It is so bright that Ptolemy listed it as a single star; Edmond Halley recognised it as something else in 1677. But Omega Centauri’s stars span a range of ages and chemical makeups, so they did not all form at once. That suggests it is the leftover core of a small galaxy that the Milky Way tore apart long ago.

slides.alt: A dense field of thousands of red, blue and white stars, each drifting slowly in its own direction, like a swarm of bees.
slides.caption: Computer model based on Hubble measurements: stars in the core of Omega Centauri moving over the next 10,000 years, projected from how far each shifted between 2002 and 2006.
slides.credit: NASA, ESA, J. Anderson and R. van der Marel (STScI) · CC BY 4.0 · excerpt

slides.label: stars in Omega Centauri, the Milky Way’s biggest globular cluster
slides.text: Together they weigh about 4 million Suns. The cluster is about 17,000 light-years away and around 12 billion years old.

slides.prompt: In the crowded core of Omega Centauri, how far apart are neighbouring stars, on average?
slides.detail: Hubble can still pick them apart: astronomers measured the motions of more than 100,000 stars in the core, which is how the clip was made.

slides.heading: The leading idea for how it formed

steps.label: A small galaxy strays close to the Milky Way
Gravity strips away its outer stars
It now orbits our galaxy as Omega Centauri

events.text: Ptolemy lists it as a star on the centaur’s back
Edmond Halley lists it as a non-stellar object
Hubble data track the motions of 100,000+ stars
Fast stars hint at a hidden black hole, a claim later questioned

slides.question: Why do astronomers think Omega Centauri was once the core of a small galaxy?
options: Its stars differ in age and makeup
It is shaped like a spiral
slides.explanation: Its stars span a range of ages and of metallicities, the amounts of elements heavier than helium, which suggests they did not all form at the same time.
